The peak is extracted below rather than estimated by eye, since a specific coordinate is more useful for the public-safety discussion.


Show peak-location extraction code
kde_df <- as.data.frame(kde_kapuas_fixed_m)
peak_row <- kde_df[which.max(kde_df$value), ]
peak_row$value_per_km2 <- peak_row$value * 1e6

peak_sf <- st_as_sf(peak_row, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32750) |>
  st_transform(4326)

st_coordinates(peak_sf)


            X         Y
[1,] 114.1462 -2.021626


Show peak-location extraction code
peak_row$value_per_km2


[1] 7.685024


The surface shows a single dominant hotspot at approximately 114.146°E, 2.022°S, reaching 7.69 fires/km², more than triple any other elevated area. Beyond it, a chain of smaller patches (roughly 1 to 2 fires/km²) follows a similar north-south alignment. This refines the raw-point impression from the candidate maps. The corridor-like appearance reflects a loose alignment of several distinct clusters anchored by one much larger hotspot, not a single continuous band of uniformly elevated intensity.






ImportantIntensity is not risk



This surface shows where detections are concentrated, not risk. A high-intensity pixel could reflect more accessible terrain, where fires are both more likely to be started and more reliably detected, rather than worse underlying hazard. Whether the hotspot and surrounding patches represent statistically distinguishable clustering is addressed in Second-Order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis, and the concentration-versus-risk distinction is developed in the public-safety section.




5.3 Testing for Complete Spatial Randomness
The KDE surface shows where intensity is visually elevated but does not test whether the pattern departs from a homogeneous Poisson process. A quadrat count test does. The window is partitioned into a grid, observed counts are compared with those expected under CSR, and a chi-squared statistic summarises the discrepancy. Vadrevu et al. (2008) applied this approach, with nearest-neighbour analysis and Ripley’s K, to satellite fire detections in India. That study is a methodological precedent here, matching this one in data type and analytical intent though not geography.


Show quadrat test code
kapuas_quadrat_counts <- quadratcount(kapuas_ppp, nx = 5, ny = 14)
kapuas_quadrat_test <- quadrat.test(kapuas_ppp, nx = 5, ny = 14)

kapuas_quadrat_test



    Chi-squared test of CSR using quadrat counts

data:  kapuas_ppp
X2 = 3785.9, df = 45, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Quadrats: 46 tiles (irregular windows)




Show quadrat plot code
plot(unmark(kapuas_ppp), pch = 20, cex = 0.3, cols = "grey50",
     main = "Quadrat Counts of Fire Detections")
plot(kapuas_quadrat_counts, add = TRUE, col = "red", cex = 0.8)















NoteInterpreting the quadrat test result



The test rejects CSR decisively (X² = 3785.9, df = 45, p < 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶). The grid has 46 tiles rather than the nominal 70 because only tiles overlapping Kapuas’s boundary are counted. With 1,849 points even minor departures from uniformity would be significant, so the extreme p-value is expected rather than notable. The result confirms that the non-uniformity in the KDE surface is genuine rather than a bandwidth or rendering artefact.
The KDE peak falls within the highest-count tile (412 detections), confirmed with inside.owin() rather than by eye. This agreement holds only at the tile’s resolution (561.9km², roughly 25km × 24km), since a count method cannot locate anything more finely. The two methods agree on which broad area is busiest, not on an exact point.




5.4 Temporal Profile of Fire Activity
Task 2 permits investigating how intensity varies across space and time, and the Temporal Study Window deferred this until the first-order spatial pattern had been examined.
Kalimantan’s dry season, and the associated peak in peatland fire activity, is documented as typically occurring from August to October, driven by El Niño-linked drought lowering peat groundwater levels (Sulaiman et al., 2023). This study’s window extends into the front edge of that peak, so a weekly count was produced to check for a comparable late-season increase.


Show weekly count aggregation code
weekly_counts <- kapuas_fires_sf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(week_start = as.Date(cut(acq_date, "week"))) |>
  count(week_start, name = "n_fires")

range(weekly_counts$week_start)


[1] "2026-01-12" "2026-09-07"


Show weekly count aggregation code
nrow(weekly_counts)


[1] 17


Show weekly count aggregation code
sum(weekly_counts$n_fires)


[1] 1849


Show weekly count aggregation code
tail(weekly_counts, 3)


# A tibble: 3 × 2
  week_start n_fires
  <date>       <int>
1 2026-08-24     623
2 2026-08-31     378
3 2026-09-07     261


Collection ended 11 September rather than at a week boundary, so the final bin is printed above before interpreting the chart. A partial final week could otherwise be misread as a genuine decline.


Show plotting code
p_temporal <- ggplot(weekly_counts, aes(x = week_start, y = n_fires)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = as.Date("2026-08-01"), xmax = as.Date("2026-09-11"),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "orange", alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_col(fill = "firebrick", alpha = 0.8, width = 6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2026-08-01"), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2026-08-03"), y = max(weekly_counts$n_fires) * 1.02,
           label = "Documented dry-season onset (Aug-Oct)", hjust = 0,
           size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly Fire Detection Counts in Kapuas, Jan-Sep 2026",
    subtitle = "Shaded region marks the dry-season window documented in the peatland literature",
    x = NULL, y = "Fire detections per week"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

ggsave("data/kapuas_weekly_fire_counts.png", p_temporal, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 150)

p_temporal











Show partial-week normalization code
weekly_counts <- weekly_counts |>
  mutate(
    week_end = pmin(week_start + 6, as.Date("2026-09-11")),
    n_days = as.integer(week_end - week_start) + 1,
    fires_per_day = round(n_fires / n_days, 1)
  )

tail(weekly_counts, 3)


# A tibble: 3 × 5
  week_start n_fires week_end   n_days fires_per_day
  <date>       <int> <date>      <dbl>         <dbl>
1 2026-08-24     623 2026-08-30      7          89  
2 2026-08-31     378 2026-09-06      7          54  
3 2026-09-07     261 2026-09-11      5          52.2


Weekly counts rise in a near step-function from early August, consistent with the documented dry-season onset (Sulaiman et al., 2023). January to July was minimal and sporadic apart from two small bursts in mid-January and early April, before activity peaked at 623 detections (89.0 fires/day) in the week of 24 August.
The next full week (31 August to 6 September) recorded 378 detections (54.0 fires/day), a genuine drop of roughly 39% in daily intensity. The final bin (7 to 11 September) covers only 5 days, so its 261 detections look like a further steep fall, but normalised this is 52.2 fires/day, essentially unchanged. After its peak, activity plateaued at roughly 52 to 54 fires/day rather than continuing to taper.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
6 Second-Order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis
First-order analysis established that Kapuas’s intensity is strongly non-uniform, so testing against a flat-CSR null can only confirm what is already known. The decisive question for an inhomogeneous process such as wildfire is narrower: is there clustering beyond what the intensity surface already explains? Only the intensity-adjusted methods (Kinhom, Ginhom, Finhom) can answer this.
The homogeneous methods come first because they provide the baseline the adjusted result is measured against. Kinhom’s central finding is a residual, and a residual cannot be interpreted without the unadjusted departure it is taken from. The 12.4km characteristic scale used in the public-safety discussion also comes only from the standard L-function. Because the two stages differ solely in their null model, running both also serves as a sensitivity analysis.
This section is organised as a two-stage escalation of the null model, with Stage 2 carrying the interpretive weight.






NoteWhy every envelope test here is global (rank), not pointwise



Every envelope test in this section is global (nrank = 1, global = TRUE) rather than pointwise. A pointwise envelope controls the error rate only at a single distance r chosen in advance. Inspecting a curve across a range of distances, as every interpretation here does, amounts to many simultaneous comparisons, so the true error rate can far exceed the nominal level (Loosmore & Ford, 2006; Myllymäki et al., 2017). The global rank test gives a single valid significance level across the whole curve, and is applied uniformly so no method is held to a lower standard.



6.1 Stage 1 Baseline: Departure from Complete Spatial Randomness

6.1.1 G-Function: Nearest-Neighbour Distance Distribution






NoteMethod card: G-function



Question. Independent of where intensity is high, are individual fire events on average closer to their nearest neighbour than CSR would produce? This is separate from first-order intensity, since a pattern can have non-uniform intensity while still showing CSR-like spacing within each dense region.
Method. \(G(r)\) estimates the cumulative distribution of nearest-neighbour distances, the proportion of events with a nearest neighbour within distance \(r\). Computed via Gest().
Assumptions. The CSR reference assumes a homogeneous Poisson process, constant intensity and independent events. First-order analysis established Kapuas’s intensity is not homogeneous, so a direct CSR comparison risks attributing intensity-driven clustering to genuine point interaction. Stage 2 addresses this.
Null model. CSR via Monte Carlo simulation, 999 homogeneous Poisson patterns within the same owin, global rank envelope.
Edge correction. Border correction, which restricts the estimate to points far enough from the boundary to have their true nearest neighbour observed, without assuming anything about behaviour beyond the window (Baddeley et al., 2015).




Show G-function estimation code
G_kapuas <- Gest(kapuas_ppp, correction = "border")

plot(G_kapuas, main = "G-function: Kapuas Fire Detections")











Show CSR envelope simulation code
set.seed(1234)
G_kapuas_csr <- envelope(kapuas_ppp, Gest, correction = "border", nsim = 999,
                          nrank = 1, global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

plot(G_kapuas_csr, main = "G-function vs. CSR Envelope (999 simulations, global test)")











Show parameter extraction code
attr(G_kapuas, "alim")


[1]    0.000 1215.424


Show parameter extraction code
max(G_kapuas$r)


[1] 5815.863




Show gap verification code within reliable range
alim_g <- attr(G_kapuas, "alim")
r_vals_g <- G_kapuas_csr$r
gap_g <- G_kapuas_csr$obs - G_kapuas_csr$hi

within_alim_g <- r_vals_g <= alim_g[2]
sum(within_alim_g)


[1] 108


Show gap verification code within reliable range
gap_within_g <- gap_g[within_alim_g]
sum(gap_within_g <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] 10


Show gap verification code within reliable range
r_within_g <- r_vals_g[within_alim_g]
r_within_g[gap_within_g <= 0]


 [1]   0.00000  11.35911  22.71821  34.07732  45.43643  56.79553  68.15464
 [8]  79.51375  90.87285 102.23196


Show gap verification code within reliable range
gap_within_g[gap_within_g <= 0]


 [1] -0.057861377 -0.057905294 -0.055870188 -0.051745441 -0.049882326
 [6] -0.042680925 -0.034441188 -0.029032800 -0.023711682 -0.006521137


The reliable range extends to 1215.42m (spatstat’s automatically selected alim). Estimates are computed to 5815.86m but not plotted beyond that range, because the border correction’s usable sample shrinks as distance grows.
Within that range the observed curve lies outside the CSR envelope at 98 of 108 tested distances. The ten exceptions are all at the origin end, from r = 0 (where G(0) = 0 by definition) out to r ≈ 102m, with the gap narrowing from -0.058 to -0.007. This is expected rather than a weakening of the result. MODIS fire pixels are roughly 1km across, so nearest-neighbour distances below about 100m are rare however strongly clustered the pattern is, and neither curve has had room to diverge. From r ≈ 114m to the 1215.42m limit the observed curve stays above the envelope without exception. Fire events are therefore systematically closer to their nearest neighbour than CSR would produce, consistent with the hotspot-and-satellite-cluster structure in the KDE surface, and this holds under the stricter global test.
A small, sharp step near r ≈ 950 to 1000m, close to the upper edge of the reliable range, is likely an artefact of the border correction’s shrinking sample rather than a real feature.


6.1.2 F-Function: Empty-Space Distance Distribution






NoteMethod card: F-function



Question. G showed fire events are closer to each other than CSR predicts. F asks the complementary question from the opposite direction. Are random locations within Kapuas also close to a fire event, or are large stretches far from any fire? Together the two distinguish patterns that look similar on a map but mean different things: strong clustering with genuinely empty gaps (both depart) versus fires locally close together but still reachable from most of the study area (G departs, F stays closer).
Method. \(F(r)\) estimates the cumulative distribution of distances from fixed reference points, not the events themselves, to the nearest observed event. Computed via Fest().
Assumptions. Same as G. The CSR reference assumes a homogeneous Poisson process, which does not hold for Kapuas, and is interpreted with that caveat.
Null model. CSR, 999 simulations, global rank envelope.
Edge correction. correction = "best", selecting the most appropriate method for the pattern rather than committing in advance (Baddeley et al., 2015).




Show F-function estimation code
F_kapuas <- Fest(kapuas_ppp, correction = "best")

plot(F_kapuas, main = "F-function: Kapuas Fire Detections")











Show CSR envelope simulation code
set.seed(1234)
F_kapuas_csr <- envelope(kapuas_ppp, Fest, correction = "best", nsim = 999,
                          nrank = 1, global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

plot(F_kapuas_csr, main = "F-function vs. CSR Envelope (999 simulations, global test)")











Show parameter extraction code
attr(F_kapuas, "alim")


[1]    0.000 5855.694


Show parameter extraction code
max(F_kapuas$r)


[1] 5855.694




Show gap verification code within reliable range
alim_f <- attr(F_kapuas, "alim")
r_vals_f <- F_kapuas_csr$r
gap_f <- F_kapuas_csr$lo - F_kapuas_csr$obs  

within_alim_f <- r_vals_f <= alim_f[2]
sum(within_alim_f)


[1] 25


Show gap verification code within reliable range
gap_within_f <- gap_f[within_alim_f]
sum(gap_within_f <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] 3


Show gap verification code within reliable range
r_within_f <- r_vals_f[within_alim_f]
r_within_f[gap_within_f <= 0]


[1]   0.0000 243.9872 487.9745


Show gap verification code within reliable range
gap_within_f[gap_within_f <= 0]


[1] -0.04789486 -0.04474675 -0.02153568


Unlike G, F’s reliable range covers its full domain (0 to 5855.69m). The Kaplan-Meier correction, selected automatically by correction = "best", does not lose sample at larger distances the way border correction does.
The observed F lies below the CSR envelope at 22 of the 25 tested distances. The three exceptions are r = 0 (trivial, F(0) = 0 by definition) and two short distances, r ≈ 244m and r ≈ 488m, where the observed curve sits only fractionally above the lower bound (gaps of -0.045 and -0.022). Beyond r ≈ 488m the observed curve departs below the envelope without exception. Read with G, this completes the picture. Fires sit closer to each other than CSR predicts, and random locations sit further from the nearest fire. Clustering produces exactly this pair of effects, because pulling points together leaves other areas emptier.
By 5.86km, observed F reaches about 0.75 against a CSR value near 1.0. Roughly a quarter of Kapuas therefore lies more than 5.86km from any detection, a far larger fire-free area than randomness would produce.


6.1.3 K- and L-Functions: Clustering Across Distance Scales






NoteMethod card: K- and L-functions



Question. G and F established that clustering exists and is not confined to one small scale. K, and its variance-stabilised transform L, addresses the remaining question. At what distances is clustering strongest, and does the departure from CSR grow, shrink or hold constant as scale increases? This connects the statistical finding to something spatially actionable.
Method. \(K(r)\) counts the expected number of further events within distance r of a typical event, normalised by intensity. \(L(r) = \sqrt{K(r)/\pi} - r\) stabilises variance and makes deviations easier to read, since under CSR it is flat at zero. Computed via Kest(), with L derived from the K envelope.
Assumptions. Same CSR caveat as G and F. This matters more for K/L, which are more directly sensitive to intensity inhomogeneity being mistaken for point interaction, and is exactly what Stage 2 resolves.
Null model. CSR, global rank envelope.
Edge correction. Ripley (isotropic) correction (Baddeley et al., 2015).




Show K-function estimation code
K_kapuas <- Kest(kapuas_ppp, correction = "Ripley")

plot(K_kapuas, main = "K-function: Kapuas Fire Detections")











Show CSR envelope simulation code
set.seed(1234)
K_kapuas_csr <- envelope(kapuas_ppp, Kest, correction = "Ripley", nsim = 19,
                          nrank = 1, global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

plot(K_kapuas_csr, main = "K-function vs. CSR Envelope (19 simulations)")















NoteA note on simulation count for this envelope



The code runs 19 simulations (nsim = 19), giving a global rank envelope test at α ≈ 0.10. The K/L results below, including the ~12.4km characteristic distance, were originally established with a 99-simulation run under the same "Ripley" correction (α ≈ 0.02), which took roughly 30 minutes at this sample size. Re-running at nsim = 99 reproduces the result at finer resolution. nsim = 19 is substituted for faster reproducibility while preserving the same conclusion. The observed curve is unaffected by simulation count, and only the envelope’s critical values change.




Show L-function derivation code
L_kapuas_csr <- K_kapuas_csr
L_kapuas_csr$obs  <- sqrt(K_kapuas_csr$obs  / pi) - K_kapuas_csr$r
L_kapuas_csr$theo <- sqrt(K_kapuas_csr$theo / pi) - K_kapuas_csr$r
L_kapuas_csr$lo   <- sqrt(K_kapuas_csr$lo   / pi) - K_kapuas_csr$r
L_kapuas_csr$hi   <- sqrt(K_kapuas_csr$hi   / pi) - K_kapuas_csr$r

par(mar = c(7, 4, 4, 2))

plot(L_kapuas_csr, main = "L-function vs. CSR Envelope (derived from K)",
     ylab = "L(r) - r   (0 = complete spatial randomness)", legend = FALSE)

legend("bottom", inset = c(0, -0.35), xpd = TRUE, horiz = TRUE, bty = "n",
       legend = c(expression(hat(L)[obs](r)), expression(L[theo](r)),
                  expression(hat(L)[hi](r)), expression(hat(L)[lo](r))),
       col = c("black", "red", "grey", "grey"),
       lty = c(1, 2, 1, 1))















TipReading an L-function plot: why the reference line sits flat on zero



Because the L transform subtracts r, complete spatial randomness maps onto the horizontal line at zero exactly. Under CSR, \(L(r) = r\), so \(L(r) - r = 0\) by construction at every distance. The flat theoretical line is the intended baseline, not a curve that has been flattened. The simulation envelope around it has genuine nonzero width but appears visually compressed against zero, because the observed departure is orders of magnitude larger, exceeding 10,000 at its peak. This is the point of the transform. It converts “is the observed curve meaningfully above the theoretical one” into the easier visual question “is the black line above zero”.




Show parameter extraction code
attr(K_kapuas, "alim")


[1]     0.00 31230.37


Show parameter extraction code
max(K_kapuas$r)


[1] 31230.37


Show parameter extraction code
range(K_kapuas_csr$r)


[1]     0.00 31230.37




Show peak-distance extraction code
peak_idx <- which.max(L_kapuas_csr$obs)
peak_r <- L_kapuas_csr$r[peak_idx]
peak_val <- L_kapuas_csr$obs[peak_idx]

peak_r


[1] 12382.35


Show peak-distance extraction code
peak_val


[1] 10108.56


Show peak-distance extraction code
min(L_kapuas_csr$obs - L_kapuas_csr$hi)


[1] -3031.203


The observed L-function exceeds the envelope at 501 of the 512 non-zero distances tested across the 0 to 31.23km range. The eleven exceptions are confined to the shortest distances, before the curve climbs clear of the band, after which it remains outside the envelope for the entire remaining range. The departure peaks at r = 12.38km, where L(r) - r reaches 10,108.56m, which is Kapuas’s characteristic clustering scale. Beyond the peak the curve declines gradually but stays well clear of the envelope.
Because Kapuas’s intensity is already known to be non-uniform, part of this departure may reflect that variation rather than point-to-point clustering. Stage 1 cannot resolve this, so Stage 2 addresses it directly.



6.2 Stage 2 Primary Evidence: Departure from an Intensity-Adjusted Null
Stage 1 tested Kapuas against a null that first-order analysis had already falsified. Stage 2 replaces it with a null built from Kapuas’s own estimated intensity, so any remaining departure reflects point interaction rather than intensity variation. Kinhom, Ginhom and Finhom revisit Stage 1’s three questions using different statistical constructions against the same reference, which lets them triangulate the result.

6.2.1 Constructing the Reference Intensity
All three methods use one shared reference intensity \(\lambda(u)\): the metre-scale fixed-bandwidth KDE surface (kde_kapuas_fixed_m), the primary sensitivity-checked estimate from the first-order analysis, which matches kapuas_ppp’s units. Sharing one reference keeps the three results comparable.
Kinhom weights each point by \(1/\lambda(u)\), so \(\lambda(u)\) must be positive everywhere. With a 1.113km bandwidth across a regency roughly 340km long, large areas have density at or near zero.


Show zero-pixel diagnostic code
sum(kde_kapuas_fixed_m$v == 0, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] 15444


Show zero-pixel diagnostic code
range(kde_kapuas_fixed_m$v[kde_kapuas_fixed_m$v > 0], na.rm = TRUE)


[1] 5.212586e-27 7.685024e-06


15,444 pixels were exactly zero, and other values fell as low as 5.21 × 10⁻²⁷, which is underflow from the Gaussian tail rather than real density. CSR simulations place points in these areas too, so both break the \(1/\lambda\) weighting. The surface was floored at 1% of its mean. A floor relative to the maximum was tried first, but it sat roughly six orders of magnitude below the surface’s typical scale, giving sparse-area points implausible weights and destabilising the envelope. The mean-based floor keeps those weights plausible while avoiding zeros.


Show mean-density diagnostic code
mean(kde_kapuas_fixed_m$v, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] 1.084873e-07




Show lambda flooring code
kde_mean <- mean(kde_kapuas_fixed_m$v, na.rm = TRUE)
kde_floor <- kde_mean * 0.01

kde_kapuas_fixed_m_floored <- eval.im(pmax(kde_kapuas_fixed_m, kde_floor))

kde_floor


[1] 1.084873e-09


Show lambda flooring code
range(kde_kapuas_fixed_m_floored)


[1] 1.084873e-09 7.685024e-06


Show lambda flooring code
# Ginhom/Finhom envelopes require an lmin strictly below the surface minimum
lmin_safe <- min(kde_kapuas_fixed_m_floored) * 0.999
lmin_safe


[1] 1.083788e-09


Kinhom also needs normpower, which rescales the estimate to reduce bias under strong inhomogeneity. spatstat keeps normpower = 1 as the default only for backward compatibility and recommends normpower = 2 here. With 15,444 pixels at zero before flooring, Kapuas clearly qualifies, so normpower = 2 is used in both the estimate and its envelope.






NoteA shared circularity



All three methods assume \(\lambda(u)\) approximates the true intensity. Because that estimate comes from the same 1,849 points being tested, each asks whether there is clustering beyond what this estimate explains, not beyond the true, unobservable intensity. envelope() warns about the same issue: a fixed lambda departs from the method’s strict assumptions (this warning is suppressed in the rendered output).
This is standard practice for the diagnostic (Baddeley et al., 2015) and does not invalidate the results, but it does mean they describe the shape of the remaining dependency rather than giving fully independent confirmation. It applies equally to all three methods and is not repeated below.




6.2.2 Inhomogeneous K-Function






NoteMethod card: Kinhom



Question. Is the large Stage 1 departure genuine point-to-point clustering, or substantially just the K-function correctly detecting Kapuas’s already-known intensity variation expressed differently?
Method. Kinhom() generalises Ripley’s K to a spatially varying intensity \(\lambda(u)\) by weighting each pairwise distance contribution by the local intensity at each point (Baddeley et al., 2000). It remains second-order in the same sense as standard K, differing only in whether the reference intensity is constant or varying (Baddeley et al., 2015).
Null model. An inhomogeneous Poisson process with \(\lambda(u)\) set to the floored KDE surface, a null that already incorporates Kapuas’s known spatial concentration.
Edge correction. Translation, not the isotropic correction used for standard K. This is a deliberate departure rather than an inconsistency. For inhomogeneous clustered patterns, translation correction is the better-supported choice in the literature, while isotropic correction is both less appropriate under strong inhomogeneity and, at 1,849 points (beyond spatstat’s ~1,000-point threshold), substantially more demanding computationally.




Show inhomogeneous K-function estimation code
Kinhom_kapuas <- Kinhom(kapuas_ppp, lambda = kde_kapuas_fixed_m_floored,
                         correction = "translate", normpower = 2)

plot(Kinhom_kapuas, main = "Inhomogeneous K-function: Kapuas Fire Detections")











Show CSR envelope simulation code
set.seed(1234)
Kinhom_kapuas_csr <- envelope(kapuas_ppp, Kinhom, lambda = kde_kapuas_fixed_m_floored,
                               correction = "translate", normpower = 2, nsim = 99,
                               nrank = 1, global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE,
                               simulate = expression(rpoispp(kde_kapuas_fixed_m_floored)))

plot(Kinhom_kapuas_csr, main = "Inhomogeneous K-function vs. Intensity-Adjusted Envelope (99 sims)")











Show gap analysis code
gap <- Kinhom_kapuas_csr$obs - Kinhom_kapuas_csr$hi
r_vals <- Kinhom_kapuas_csr$r

# Does the observed curve ever dip inside the envelope 
any(gap <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] TRUE


Show gap analysis code
sum(gap <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] 501


Show gap analysis code
# Range and location of the minimum gap (closest approach to the envelope)
min(gap, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] -1072682837


Show gap analysis code
r_vals[which.min(gap)]


[1] 0


Show gap analysis code
# Range and location of the maximum gap (widest departure)
max(gap, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] -267981745


Show gap analysis code
r_vals[which.max(gap)]


[1] 31227.75


Unlike the standard K/L-function, Kinhom shows no sustained departure. The observed curve never exceeds the intensity-adjusted envelope’s upper bound at any of the 501 tested distances, remaining inside or below the band throughout.
This substantially revises the Stage 1 finding rather than merely qualifying it. Once the known intensity surface is the reference, almost none of the large K/L departure from flat CSR survives. Kapuas’s known fire-prone geography accounts for essentially all of the second-moment clustering structure Stage 1 detected, at both short and long range.


6.2.3 Inhomogeneous G- and F-Functions






NoteMethod card: Ginhom and Finhom



Question. The ambiguity Kinhom resolved for the second-moment measure applies equally to nearest-neighbour and empty-space distances. Do the Stage 1 G and F departures survive intensity adjustment? Because these use a different construction from Kinhom, they provide independent triangulation rather than restatement.
Method. Ginhom() and Finhom() generalise the nearest-neighbour and empty-space functions to a spatially varying reference intensity, following Lieshout (2011).
Null model. An inhomogeneous Poisson process using the same floored KDE surface as Kinhom, so all three test against one reference.
Parameters and edge correction. Both use a fixed border correction, with no user-selectable option unlike Kest()/Kinhom(). Both require lmin, the minimum possible intensity over the domain. The point estimates use kde_floor directly, while the envelopes require a value strictly below the floored surface’s minimum and therefore use lmin_safe (0.1% lower). This is a technical requirement of the function, not a change in the reference intensity.




Show Ginhom and Finhom estimation code
Ginhom_kapuas <- Ginhom(kapuas_ppp, lambda = kde_kapuas_fixed_m_floored, lmin = kde_floor)
Finhom_kapuas <- Finhom(kapuas_ppp, lambda = kde_kapuas_fixed_m_floored, lmin = kde_floor)



Ginhom estimateFinhom estimate

























Unlike the homogeneous G-function, whose sign convention is well established, spatstat’s documentation for Ginhom does not state which direction indicates clustering versus regularity for the reweighted version. This was confirmed with a control test rather than assumed. Ginhom computed under a flat, constant intensity should behave equivalently to ordinary Gest, since reweighting becomes trivial when the reference does not vary.


Show sign-convention verification code
flat_lambda_val <- kapuas_ppp$n / area.owin(kapuas_owin)
flat_lambda_vec <- rep(flat_lambda_val, kapuas_ppp$n)

Ginhom_flat_check <- Ginhom(kapuas_ppp, lambda = flat_lambda_vec)

flat_check <- data.frame(
  r = Ginhom_flat_check$r,
  gap = Ginhom_flat_check$bord - Ginhom_flat_check$theo
)


mean(flat_check$gap > 0, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] 0.6003899


Show sign-convention verification code
sum(flat_check$gap > 0, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] 308


Show sign-convention verification code
sum(flat_check$gap < 0, na.rm = TRUE)


[1] 204


Show sign-convention verification code
flat_check[round(seq(1, nrow(flat_check), length.out = 8)), ]


            r          gap

6.2.4 What Survives Adjustment
All three methods agree with each other, unlike the mixed picture Stage 1 alone would suggest:

Kinhom: never exceeds the intensity-adjusted envelope at any of 501 tested distances. No departure at any scale.
Finhom: departs at only 10 of 95 tested distances, maximum effect size −0.0155.
Ginhom: departs at only 4 of 95 tested distances, maximum effect size −0.0057.

Once point interaction is separated from intensity variation, Kapuas’s fire pattern shows almost no residual clustering or regularity beyond what the intensity surface already predicts. The large departures Stage 1 found against flat CSR are attributable overwhelmingly to non-uniform intensity, not to fires interacting with, triggering or avoiding each other.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
7 Integrated Findings and Discussion

7.1 What Each Level of Analysis Reveals
First-order. The KDE surface identifies a single dominant hotspot at 114.146°E, 2.022°S reaching 7.69 fires/km², more than triple any other elevated area, alongside smaller 1 to 2 fires/km² patches on a similar north-south alignment. The quadrat test confirms this non-uniformity is genuine (X² = 3785.9, df = 45, p < 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶), and its highest-count tile (412 detections) contains the KDE peak, confirmed by containment testing. The temporal profile adds the dimension the brief permits alongside space, with activity concentrated overwhelmingly in the final six weeks (Sulaiman et al., 2023).
Second-order. Stage 1 established that this concentration reflects more than visual clustering. G and F depart from CSR in complementary directions across almost their entire reliable ranges, and K/L confirm this holds out to 31.2km, peaking at 12.38km. Stage 2 shows the departure is overwhelmingly attributable to non-uniform intensity rather than point interaction, since Kinhom, Ginhom and Finhom all fall within their intensity-adjusted envelopes at the overwhelming majority of tested distances.


7.2 Complementarity Between the Two Levels
The two levels answer different halves of the same question. First-order analysis identifies where intensity is elevated and how strongly, but cannot distinguish event-to-event interaction from events simply occurring more often in an already fire-prone location. Second-order analysis fills that gap. Stage 1 establishes that interaction exists beyond flat randomness, and Stage 2 separates how much survives once the known intensity pattern is held constant.
That is what makes the finding more than descriptive. Kinhom, Ginhom and Finhom converge on the same conclusion despite three different statistical constructions. This replaces “fires are clustered” with something more precise and more cautious: Kapuas’s second-order structure is substantially explained by its documented fire-prone geography, not by fire-to-fire interaction. Only comparing Stage 1 against Stage 2 makes that distinction visible.


7.3 Cross-Method Summary

The KDE peak falls inside the quadrat grid’s highest-count tile (412 detections, 561.9km²), confirmed by containment testing rather than visual estimation.


7.4 Consistency Across Analytical Views
The conclusion that Kapuas’s fires are clustered rather than random, tested against flat CSR, holds across the quadrat test, KDE, G, F and K/L. KDE and quadrat counts agree on the hotspot’s broad location, though only at the coarser method’s resolution, since a discrete grid cannot resolve location more finely than its 561.9km² tile.
Stage 1 and Stage 2 diverge in a way that is informative rather than a weakness. Stage 1’s homogeneous methods reject flat CSR decisively, while Stage 2’s intensity-adjusted methods each independently find almost no departure from a properly-specified inhomogeneous null. The divergence is between the two stages, and it has a clear explanation. Stage 1’s large departure was driven substantially by intensity variation that Stage 2 correctly absorbs into its reference.


7.5 Assumptions and Limitations
These are consolidated in Limitations rather than repeated here. In brief: Stage 1’s CSR reference does not describe Kapuas, which is why Stage 2 exists. Stage 2 fixes that but is circular, since its reference intensity comes from the same data being tested. The G-function’s reliable range stops at 1.22km because of its border correction. The pooled cross-sectional treatment sets aside a strongly concentrated temporal pattern, examined in the Bonus extension. Every finding describes detected fire events, so lower measured intensity can mean less reliable detection rather than less fire.






TipSensitivity checks ran throughout



Sensitivity analysis was built into the workflow rather than left to this section. Fixed bandwidth was tested against adaptive, bw.ppl() against bw.diggle(), and every homogeneous test against its inhomogeneous counterpart, which is what the Stage 1 and Stage 2 structure is for. These comparisons did real work. Switching from a flat-CSR null to a properly-specified intensity-adjusted null overturned the Stage 1 clustering conclusion for all three methods.




7.6 Alternative Explanations for the Observed Pattern
The clustered pattern is consistent with several mechanisms that fire-detection data alone cannot distinguish.
One is genuine spatial contagion, with fires spreading to or triggering nearby fires, producing the short-range G/F signature observed. A second is a shared driver. Proximity to roads and rivers is documented as a fire-risk factor in Kapuas, associated with human land clearing (Thoha et al., 2019), so accessible terrain could attract the activity that starts fires without fires causing fires. A third, harder to rule out, is detection bias. If satellite coverage or cloud-free days vary spatially, an area could appear as a hotspot partly through better observation.
The second-order analysis lends weight to the shared-driver mechanism. Once the intensity surface, itself a proxy for the underlying fire-prone terrain, is used as the reference, almost none of the raw clustering signal remains unexplained. A covariate-based model (distance to river, road, or BPBD facility) would be needed to confirm the driver itself rather than the intensity surface standing in for it. Those covariates were identified as relevant when the study window was defined, but the GIS layers have not been acquired, so this remains future work.
Ginhom’s small residual departure (4 of 95 distances, maximum effect −0.0057) is too weak to support a claim of nearest-neighbour regularity. It is more consistent with ordinary Monte Carlo variability under a global test spanning many distances than with a real mechanism, so no specific explanation is proposed.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
8 Spatio-Temporal Extension (Bonus/Value-Added)






NoteMethod card: period-split spatio-temporal comparison



Question. The main analysis pools the full window into one cross-section even though activity concentrates in the final six weeks. Does the pooled pattern hide two distinct spatial regimes, a sparse period before the dry-season onset and a concentrated surge after it, or does the same pattern simply intensify uniformly? Spatio-temporal treatments of Kalimantan hotspot data exist in the literature (Lestari et al., 2016; Sahitya, 2021), typically across multiple fire seasons rather than within one.
Method. The window splits at the step-change boundary from the temporal profile (1 August), giving a quiet period (1 Jan to 31 Jul, 58 points) and a surge period (1 Aug to 11 Sep, 1,791 points). Each uses the same core methods as the main analysis, fixed-bandwidth KDE via bw.ppl() and the L-function against CSR, so any difference reflects the pattern rather than the method.
Assumptions and departures. Two simplifications apply here only. The second-order comparison uses the homogeneous L-function instead of the inhomogeneous suite, since building an intensity-adjusted reference from 58 points would add a second layer of estimation instability on top of an already small sample. The envelopes use correction = "border" instead of "Ripley" and 19 simulations instead of 99, for tractability. Border correction is faster at the surge period’s sample size, and 19 simulations still give a valid global rank envelope test with coarser critical values.
Null model. CSR within the same owin used throughout, applied separately to each period’s own point count.

As in the main L-function plot, the theoretical line sits at zero because \(L(r) - r = 0\) under CSR at every distance. The quiet period’s much wider, noisier envelope reflects its small sample.
Results and interpretation. The quiet period needed a much wider smoothing radius (bw.ppl() = 6.65km versus the surge period’s 1.113km, which matches the main analysis exactly since the surge holds 1,791 of 1,849 points), reflecting a sparser, more scattered distribution. Its peak (114.331°E, 1.372°S) sits 75.13km from the surge peak (114.146°E, 2.022°S, essentially the full-period hotspot), and its peak intensity (0.027 fires/km²) is roughly 289 times lower. The season’s dominant hotspot did not form where the earlier, weak activity was concentrated.
The two periods behave very differently against CSR. The surge period departs from the envelope at 478 of 513 tested distances (93.2%), a sustained and unambiguous clustering signal. The quiet period does not: its observed curve exceeds the envelope at only 4 of 513 distances, so at 58 points its pattern is not statistically distinguishable from CSR. Its nominal peak (r ≈ 14.03km, L(r) - r = 12,269.76) is larger in absolute terms than the surge’s (r ≈ 4.57km, L(r) - r = 7,776.01), but it sits inside a Monte Carlo envelope made very wide by the small sample and should not be read as evidence of a broader-scale clustering process. Only the surge period’s characteristic scale, 4.57km, is statistically supported, and it is tighter than the pooled analysis’s 12.38km.
The quiet period’s 58 points sit just above the report’s 50-point stability floor, and the L-function result shows the consequence directly. At that sample size CSR cannot be rejected, so the quiet period’s spatial structure can only be characterised descriptively through its KDE surface. The evidence that the two periods are distinct therefore rests on the first-order comparison, where it is strong: a 75.13km separation between peaks, a six-fold difference in bandwidth, and a roughly 289-fold difference in peak intensity. On that basis the dry-season surge is a spatially distinct, more tightly-clustered process rather than an intensified continuation of wherever fires already occurred.
This complicates the pooled treatment in the main analysis. The full-period hotspot and characteristic distance largely reflect the surge specifically, unsurprising since it holds 97% of points, but a spatio-temporal treatment would frame this as two regimes rather than one pattern at varying intensity. For readiness planning, response anchored to the pooled hotspot remains well-supported for the surge period it actually reflects, but should not be read as describing a quiet-period baseline.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
9 Geovisualisation and Geocommunication
Five visuals were curated from the full set produced across this report, selected to communicate the analytical findings rather than the data-preparation and study-area-selection visuals, which serve Task 1 rather than Task 5.

9.1 Fixed-Bandwidth Kernel Density Estimate


Show map redisplay code
kde_map_obj









Reveals: Fire intensity is strongly uneven across Kapuas. A single dominant hotspot at 114.146°E, 2.022°S reaches 7.69 fires/km², more than triple any other elevated area, with a chain of smaller 1 to 2 fires/km² patches on a similar north-south alignment rather than one continuous corridor.
Evidence: Fixed-bandwidth KDE (bw.ppl() = 1.113km), corroborated by two independent checks: a quadrat test rejecting CSR (X² = 3785.9, p < 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶), and the grid’s highest-count tile (412 detections) containing this exact peak, confirmed by containment testing.
Limitations: The surface’s shape is bandwidth-sensitive, and the adaptive alternative fragments the same hotspot. Intensity is not risk, since this records where fires were detected, which depends on satellite observation reliability as well as fire occurrence.


9.2 Does Fire Clustering Have a Characteristic Scale?


Show plot code
L_df <- data.frame(
  r_km = L_kapuas_csr$r / 1000,
  observed = L_kapuas_csr$obs,
  expected = L_kapuas_csr$theo,
  lo = L_kapuas_csr$lo,
  hi = L_kapuas_csr$hi
)

peak_r_km <- peak_r / 1000

ggplot(L_df, aes(x = r_km)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi,
                  fill = "Simulated envelope around the randomness line"),
              alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = expected,
                colour = "Complete spatial randomness (flat at 0 by construction)"),
            linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = observed, colour = "Observed pattern"), linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = peak_r_km, y = peak_val, colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = peak_r_km, y = peak_val + 700,
           label = paste0("Strongest clustering\nat ~", round(peak_r_km, 1), " km"),
           size = 3.2, hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_colour_manual(
    name = NULL,
    values = c("Observed pattern" = "black",
               "Complete spatial randomness (flat at 0 by construction)" = "firebrick")) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = NULL,
    values = c("Simulated envelope around the randomness line" = "grey70")) +
  labs(
    title = "Are Kapuas's Fires More Clustered Than Chance Would Predict?",
    subtitle = "Plotting L(r) - r puts randomness exactly on zero; height above the band is the clustering effect",
    x = "Distance between fires (km)", y = "L(r) - r   (0 = complete spatial randomness)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Reveals: The chart plots L(r) - r, a transform under which complete spatial randomness falls exactly on zero. The flat red line is the intended baseline, and the grey band around it is a real Monte Carlo envelope with genuine width that looks thin only because the observed departure is orders of magnitude larger, peaking above 10,000 near r ≈ 12.4km. Kapuas’s fires sit measurably closer together than chance across almost the entire 31.2km range tested, most strongly at about 12.4km, easing afterwards without returning inside the band.
Evidence: A global rather than pointwise envelope test, which guards against overstating significance across a range this wide.
Limitations: The comparison assumes fires could occur anywhere in Kapuas with equal likelihood, already shown false, so part of this departure may be known geography rather than fire-to-fire clustering. The next visual addresses that.


9.3 Is There Genuine Fire-to-Fire Clustering, or Just Geography?


Show plot code
Kinhom_gap_df <- data.frame(
  r_km = Kinhom_kapuas_csr$r / 1000,
  gap = Kinhom_kapuas_csr$obs - Kinhom_kapuas_csr$hi
)

ggplot(Kinhom_gap_df, aes(x = r_km, y = gap)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = pmax(gap, 0)), fill = "orange", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title = "Does Extra Clustering Remain After Accounting for Known Fire-Prone Areas?",
    subtitle = "Zero means the pattern matches an intensity-adjusted null; the curve stays at or below zero almost everywhere",
    x = "Distance between fires (km)", y = "Extra clustering beyond expected"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









Reveals: This plots the gap between the observed pattern and the upper edge of a null that already builds in Kapuas’s known fire-prone geography, so zero means exactly as expected given location. The curve never exceeds this upper bound anywhere across the tested range, remaining substantially negative even at its narrowest point. Once known geography is accounted for, no unexplained clustering signal remains at any distance.
Evidence: A formally tested departure (99 simulations, global envelope) against an intensity-adjusted reference rather than pure randomness. The absence of exceedances was verified against the underlying data rather than estimated visually.
Limitations: The reference is built from the same fire data being tested, a circularity shared by all three inhomogeneous methods. Finhom and Ginhom independently reach the same conclusion.


9.4 Temporal Profile of Fire Activity


Show plot redisplay code
p_temporal









Reveals: Fire activity is heavily concentrated in the final six weeks of the observation window rather than spread across January to September, coinciding with the documented onset of Kalimantan’s dry season.
Evidence: Weekly counts show a near step-function increase from early August, peaking at 623 detections (89.0 fires/day) in the week of 24 August. The apparent collapse in the final, shorter bar is a plateau at 52.2 fires/day once normalised for its 5-day length, matching the documented dry-season window (Sulaiman et al., 2023).
Limitations: Only one season is observed, with no multi-year baseline to confirm this is typical. The main spatial analyses pool the full window, and the quiet/surge split is examined in the Spatio-Temporal Extension at reduced power given the quiet period’s small sample.


9.5 Cross-Method Distance Comparison


Show plot redisplay code
p_synthesis_distances









Reveals: The three Stage 1 methods operate at genuinely different distances spanning roughly 1.2km to 12.4km, almost an order of magnitude. None of Stage 2’s methods appear, since none shows a sustained departure worth marking on this scale.
Evidence: All three distances are extracted directly from the fitted spatstat objects rather than estimated visually. The log scale keeps the shorter G-function distance legible next to the longer K/L peak.
Limitations: This chart reflects only Stage 1’s departure from flat CSR, which the Stage 2 analysis substantially explains away. The Stage 2 results are captured in the cross-method table instead.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
10 Public-Safety Planning and Management Implications
Evidence-supported implications. The KDE surface and quadrat test jointly locate a verified hotspot (114.146°E, 2.022°S, within a 561.9km² tile recording 412 detections), a concrete candidate for BPBD resource staging or monitoring infrastructure. Second-order analysis, once known fire-prone geography is accounted for, finds almost no residual clustering beyond that geography. This supports concentrating resources on the mapped intensity surface itself rather than planning a separate response radius for fire-to-fire spread. The temporal profile is equally actionable. Activity concentrated in the final six weeks with a step-change onset in early August supports a seasonally front-loaded posture ahead of the dry-season window rather than reacting after activity has surged.

10.1 Illustrative Response-Radius Map


Show map code
peak_sf_utm <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x = peak_row$x, y = peak_row$y),
                         coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32750)

buffer_characteristic <- st_buffer(peak_sf_utm, dist = peak_r)

kde_df_plot <- as.data.frame(kde_kapuas_terra_km2, xy = TRUE)
names(kde_df_plot)[3] <- "density"

bbox_kapuas <- st_bbox(kapuas_boundary_utm)
x_margin <- (bbox_kapuas["xmax"] - bbox_kapuas["xmin"]) * 0.45
label_x <- bbox_kapuas["xmax"] + x_margin * 0.35

anchor_characteristic <- data.frame(x = peak_row$x + peak_r, y = peak_row$y)

label_characteristic_pos <- data.frame(x = label_x, y = peak_row$y)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = kde_df_plot, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = density)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Estimated fire density (per km²)",
                        trans = "sqrt", na.value = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = kapuas_boundary_utm, fill = NA, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = buffer_characteristic, fill = NA, colour = "red3",
          linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_sf(data = peak_sf_utm, colour = "white", size = 4.5) +
  geom_sf(data = peak_sf_utm, colour = "black", size = 3) +
  geom_segment(data = anchor_characteristic,
               aes(x = x, y = y, xend = label_characteristic_pos$x,
                   yend = label_characteristic_pos$y),
               colour = "red3", linewidth = 0.4,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), ends = "first")) +
  geom_label(data = label_characteristic_pos,
             aes(x = x, y = y, label = "12.4km\ncharacteristic\nclustering scale\n(L-function)"),
             fill = "white", colour = "red3", size = 2.8, label.size = 0.3,
             hjust = 0, label.padding = unit(0.3, "lines")) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(bbox_kapuas["xmin"], bbox_kapuas["xmax"] + x_margin),
           ylim = c(bbox_kapuas["ymin"], bbox_kapuas["ymax"]),
           expand = FALSE) +
  annotation_scale(location = "bl", width_hint = 0.2) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Verified Hotspot with the Stage 1 Characteristic Clustering Radius",
       subtitle = "Radius is the Stage 1 (flat-CSR) characteristic distance; the underlying surface is the fixed-bandwidth KDE")









The circle marks the Stage 1 characteristic clustering distance around the verified peak, not an operational service area. The buffer is isotropic while Kapuas’s pattern is corridor-like, so the radius indicates scale, not the shape of a response zone. It reflects the raw departure from randomness against flat CSR, not a distance at which fire-to-fire interaction has been confirmed. The intensity-adjusted analysis found no such residual signal.


10.2 When Should Readiness Already Be in Place?


Show plot code
cumulative_df <- kapuas_fires_sf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(acq_date, name = "n_fires") |>
  arrange(acq_date) |>
  mutate(cum_n = cumsum(n_fires),
         cum_pct = cum_n / sum(n_fires) * 100)

pct_by_aug1 <- cumulative_df$cum_pct[max(which(cumulative_df$acq_date <= as.Date("2026-08-01")))]
date_90pct <- cumulative_df$acq_date[which(cumulative_df$cum_pct >= 90)[1]]

pct_by_aug1


[1] 3.190914


Show plot code
date_90pct


[1] "2026-09-10"


Show plot code
ggplot(cumulative_df, aes(x = acq_date, y = cum_pct)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2026-08-01"), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 90, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey60") +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2026-08-01"), y = 5, label = "1 Aug",
           hjust = -0.1, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(title = "Cumulative Share of the Season's Fires Over Time",
       subtitle = paste0("By 1 August, only ", round(pct_by_aug1, 1),
                          "% of the season's total fires had occurred"),
       x = NULL, y = "Cumulative % of season's fires") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









By 1 August only 3.19% of the season’s fires had occurred, and 90% was not reached until 10 September, one day before the window closes. Readiness therefore needs to be in place well before the onset date, and activity was still building rather than tapering when the data ends.
Implications requiring additional information. Whether known geography is the actual causal driver of Stage 1’s raw clustering, or merely correlates with an unobserved one, is not established here. The intensity surface accounts statistically for almost all of the second-order structure, but it is itself only a proxy for whatever makes some areas more fire-prone. Three candidate drivers were identified (road and river accessibility (Thoha et al., 2019), fire-to-fire spread, and uneven satellite detection), and this analysis cannot distinguish between them. A covariate-based model would be needed to test the first directly, so land-use or road-network policy responses should not be justified as addressing a specific cause until that model is built. BPBD facility locations were named as analytically relevant but no such distances were computed, so any claim about current response-unit proximity would be speculation.
Intensity is also not risk. A high-detection area may reflect more reliable observation rather than elevated hazard, so resource decisions should treat this surface as a starting hypothesis for field verification. This analysis covers one season, and whether 2026’s timing is typical cannot be determined without multi-year data, which matters for any commitment to permanent rather than seasonal infrastructure.
In summary, the analysis supports targeted, time-bound readiness around a specific, well-verified location and season. It does not on its own support causal land-use claims, fixed infrastructure siting, or conclusions about underlying fire risk without further field or covariate data.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
11 Limitations
This section consolidates limitations identified at the point they arose rather than introducing new ones.
Data. Near-duplicate detections (23.4% of raw records) were collapsed to one representative per location/day group using highest confidence as tie-breaker, a defensible but not uniquely correct rule. A different rule could shift counts slightly, though the spatial pattern is unlikely to be sensitive to this given the scale of clustering observed. Detection is satellite-dependent, and MODIS’s ~1km resolution and revisit geometry mean reliability varies with cloud cover, terrain accessibility and overpass timing, so lower measured intensity is not necessarily lower actual activity. This applies to every intensity- and clustering-based finding.
Coordinate system and boundary geometry. Kapuas straddles the UTM zone 49/50 boundary at 114°E, and EPSG:32750 was applied uniformly, introducing minor positional distortion for the minority of points near the western edge. The dissolved boundary contains a topological sliver (0.1457km², confirmed to contain zero fire points) that trivially reduces usable window area.
First-order analysis. KDE is bandwidth-sensitive. bw.ppl() and bw.diggle() disagreed by a factor of two, and fixed versus adaptive produced visibly different surfaces. The fixed result was retained as primary with the disagreement documented rather than resolved. The quadrat test’s extreme significance is partly a function of sample size, so the p-value’s magnitude is not informative beyond confirming non-uniformity.
Second-order analysis. Stage 1’s homogeneous tests compare against flat CSR, which does not describe Kapuas. Stage 2 addresses this using an intensity surface estimated from the same data being tested, a circularity affecting all three inhomogeneous methods. The G-function’s reliable range is truncated to 1.22km by its border correction. All three Stage 2 methods find only isolated, small-magnitude exceedances rather than a sustained departure (Kinhom 0 of 501, Ginhom 4 of 95, Finhom 10 of 95), so this analysis does not identify a robust residual signal of either clustering or regularity.
Temporal scope. The main analysis treats the full window as one pooled cross-section despite activity being concentrated in the final six weeks. The Spatio-Temporal Extension examines the quiet/surge split separately, at reduced power given the quiet period’s 58-point sample, where CSR could not be rejected.
Unresolved causal and policy questions. Whether the intensity surface that explains Stage 1’s clustering reflects road and river accessibility specifically, or some other unobserved driver, cannot be established with fire-detection data alone. Doing so would require a covariate-based model that was not built here.

3.2 Performing Moran’s I

3.2.1 Step 2A: Computing Global Moran’s I
global_moran() function is used to compute the Moran’s I value. Different from sdep package, the output is a tibble data.frame.

moranI <- global_moran(wm_q$GDPPC,
                       wm_q$nb,
                       wm_q$wt)
glimpse(moranI)

List of 2
 $ I: num 0.301
 $ K: num 7.64




3.2.2 Step 2B: Performing Global Moran’s I test
Moran’s I test will be performed instead of just computing the Moran’s I statistics. With sfdep package, Moran’s I test can be performed by using global_moran_test() as shown in the code chunk below.

global_moran_test(wm_q$GDPPC,
                       wm_q$nb,
                       wm_q$wt)

weights: listw
